el: Αργκό των νέων και του ίντερνετ
title: Youth and internet slang, texting and Greeklish

blocks.title: Who talks like this, and how the machine works
blocks.text:
This unit is about the Greek of people roughly 13 to 28 in the years 2015-2026: the *Gen Z* who grew up on Viber, Instagram and TikTok, plus the millennials who invented half of the internet habits that teenagers now find *κριντζ*. You will hear it in schoolyards, at the καφετέρια, in group chats and in every Greek TikTok comment section. You will rarely hear it from your landlord, and you should almost never produce it with your boss.

Three engines produce almost all of it:

**1. English roots + the Greek suffix -άρω.** Greek has borrowed verbs this way for centuries (from Italian: *παρκάρω, μπλοκάρω*; from English in the 90s-2000s: *τσεκάρω, σερφάρω*). Today the same suffix swallows anything the internet produces: **κριντζάρω** (cringe), **φλεξάρω** (flex), **ντισάρω** (diss), **μπιφάρω** (beef), **σκρολάρω** (scroll), **ποστάρω** (post), **τρολάρω** (troll), **λολάρω** (lol), **μπιντζάρω** (binge), **μπρικάρω** (brick: a phone that freezes). The verb is fully Greek: it conjugates in all persons and tenses, and the aorist pulls the stress back to the root: *κριντζάρω → κρίντζαρα*, *ποστάρω → πόσταρα*, *σκρολάρω → σκρόλαρα*.

**2. Bare English nouns and adjectives, usually indeclinable and neuter.** *Το κριντζ, το βάιμπ, το ποστ, το στόρι, το λάικ, το σιν (seen)*; and as predicates: *είναι πολύ κριντζ*, *είναι κουλ*. Plural, if any, is the same word: *τα στόρι σου*. Gender for people follows the person: *ο μπρο, η μπρο* (girls call each other μπρο too).

**3. Greek words with new jobs.** Old words shift meaning (**βασικός** 'basic' = conformist, no personality; **άκυρος** 'void' = awkward, off-topic, a person who keeps letting people down), get scrambled (**γκαφρά** from φράγκα 'money'; **τέπο** from ποτέ 'never') or chopped (**τέσπα** from τέλος πάντων). And the older generation's slang (**κάψα, καμένος, κάφρος, φλώρος, ξενέρωτος, τζέρτζελο**) is still in circulation, sometimes ironically.

Throughout this lesson each item carries a **status**: *current* (heard from teenagers and twenty-somethings now), *established* (everyone under 50 uses or understands it), *fading* (marks you as a millennial or older), or *unverified* (we could not confirm real use, so do not produce it).

blocks.title: Greeklish: Greek in Latin letters
blocks.text:
**Greeklish** (also *Γκρίκλις, φραγκοχιώτικα* in older jokes) is Greek typed in the Latin alphabet. It exploded in the 1990s-2000s because early phones, e-mail and chat programs could not handle Greek characters, and SMS was cheaper in Latin script. When Unicode keyboards became universal (around 2010) it retreated sharply: many forums banned it, and today a long Greeklish text looks dated or lazy. It survives in quick chats, YouTube and TikTok comments, usernames, hashtags, people typing on a foreign keyboard, and Greeks abroad.

There is **no standard**. Two philosophies compete:

- **Phonetic**: write what you hear. *πλατεία* → *platia*, *είναι* → *ine*, *ευχαριστώ* → *efxaristo*. All the *i*-sounds (η, ι, υ, ει, οι) become *i*.
- **Orthographic / visual**: keep the Greek spelling visible. *πλατεία* → *plateia*, *είναι* → *einai*, *ευχαριστώ* → *eyxaristw*. Here **w = ω** (it looks like it) and **y = υ**.

Numbers fill gaps by shape: **8 = θ** (*8elw* θέλω), **3 = ξ** (*3erw* ξέρω), **4 = ψ** (*4wmi* ψωμί), and **0** occasionally for θ. **x** usually = χ (*xara* χαρά), so ξ becomes *ks* or *3*. **h** sometimes = η (*kalh* καλή). Accents are dropped, and **?** is the English question mark, not the Greek ;.

As a reader you need to decode it; as a writer, avoid it in anything longer than a joke. In professional e-mail it reads as unprofessional.

blocks.title: How Greeks shorten words in chat
items: Drop the vowels, keep the consonants: *τίποτα → τπτ, γενικά → γνκ, περίμενε → πρμν*. If you can read the skeleton aloud and it resolves to one common word, it works.
Keep a vowel when the word would be unrecognisable without it: *ακλ* (α καλά) keeps the initial α.
No accents, no capitals, no final full stop. A final full stop in a short chat message can read as cold or angry, exactly as in English.
Question marks: Greek keyboards produce ; but many people type ? out of habit; both are understood in chat.
Abbreviations are for chat only. In e-mail, even informal e-mail to a colleague, write the words out.
Older relatives tend to type the opposite way: full sentences, full stops, sometimes ALL CAPS, and signature greetings like *Φιλιά, η μαμά*. Teenagers find this *κριντζ*; it is not rude.

blocks.title: Viber, voice notes, seen: digital manners in Greece
blocks.text:
**Viber** is the default messenger of Greece across generations: by the company's own figures it sits on over 90% of Greek smartphones, and family group chats (*το γκρουπ της οικογένειας*) with grandparents forwarding good-morning images live there. Teenagers and twenty-somethings move a lot of their social life to **Instagram** DMs and stories, and to **TikTok**; WhatsApp is more common with foreigners and for work groups. Saying *στείλε μου στο Viber* is normal even in business contexts that in other countries would use e-mail.

**Voice messages** (*φωνητικό, ηχητικό μήνυμα*) are hugely popular, especially with people who type slowly and with chatty friends; a three-minute *φωνητικό* instead of a text is common and not considered rude between friends. Some young people hate them (*μη μου στέλνεις ηχητικά, δεν μπορώ να ακούσω τώρα*): ask.

**Seen** (*μου άφησε σιν, με άφησε στο seen*) is a social event in itself: being left on seen by a crush is a classic source of *κάψα* drama, and *γκόστινγκ* (disappearing without a word) is the same thing taken to the limit.

**How 30+ Greeks react.** Parents and teachers mostly laugh at, imitate or complain about youth slang: *Μίλα ελληνικά, παιδί μου!*, *Τι είναι πάλι αυτό το κριντζ;*, *Στην εποχή μου λέγαμε...*. The press runs a regular 'dictionary of teen language for parents' and a regular panic about the 'impoverishment' of Greek (*γλωσσική φτώχεια*); linguists interviewed in those same articles usually answer that every generation tests the limits of the language, that the -άρω suffix shows Greek is healthy and creative, and that the real risk would be abandoning Greek, not decorating it with English. A parent saying *μην κριντζάρεις* to a teenager is itself a joke: the moment parents use a word, it starts to die.

blocks.title: Pronunciation
blocks.text:
**Loans are pronounced with Greek sounds.** English vowels collapse into the five Greek vowels and every letter is pronounced: *κριντζ* [krindz], *βάιμπ* [vaib], *φλεξ* [fleks], *μπρο* [bro] with a Greek tapped r, *λολ* [lol] rhyming with 'doll', never 'lole'. Final consonant clusters are often simplified: *ρισπέκτ* is often said and written *ρισπέκ*.

**Stress in -άρω verbs** sits on -ά- in the present and jumps back three syllables from the end in the past: *σκρο-ΛΑ-ρω* but *ΣΚΡΟ-λα-ρα*, *πο-ΣΤΑ-ρω* but *ΠΟ-στα-ρα*. Getting this right is what makes you sound native rather than like you are reading.

**αι in βάιμπ**: the accent (or a diaeresis in *βαϊμπάρω*) tells you the two vowels are pronounced separately [a-i], not as the digraph αι = [e].

**Reaction words carry the intonation.** *Τρελό!* and *Σοκ!* are flat and clipped, almost deadpan in ironic use; *Κριιιντζ* is drawn out with a pained face; *Άκυρο* is quick and falling, a door slamming. *Λολ* said aloud is almost always ironic.

**Spelling of loans** is unstable: *κρίντζ/κριντζ/γκριντζ*, *τσιλ/τσίλ*, *ρισπέκτ/ρισπέκ/ρησπέκτ*. Monosyllables officially take no accent (*κριντζ, μπρο*), but you will see accents everywhere online.

blocks.text:
**Common mistakes and false friends**

- **Age matters more than grammar.** Coming from a forty-year-old foreigner, *μπρο* and *τσίλαρε* sound like a dad trying to be young: funny once, painful twice. Understand everything here; produce sparingly, mostly the *established* items (*σόρι, οκ, κουλ, τσεκάρω, σαπίζω, ξενέρωσα, καμένος*).
- **κουλ is not youth slang.** It has been Greek since the 80s; using it marks nothing.
- **ξενέρωτος** has nothing to do with 'un-' + 'water' in its modern meaning: it means boring, a killjoy. *Ξενέρωσα* = I was put off / lost the mood.
- **κάφρος** comes from a racist term; **φλώρος** carries a homophobic undertone; **κάγκουρας** is class-based mockery. All three are everyday words, but know what you are saying.
- **κκ.** in formal writing means *κύριοι* (Messrs, e.g. *Προς τους κκ. Παπαδόπουλο και Γεωργίου*); in chat **κκ** means OK. Do not confuse them.
- **λολ said aloud** is ironic, not a laugh. And typing *λολ* after every sentence marks you as a millennial.
- **άκυρο** as an interjection is a blunt 'no / forget it'. With adults it can sound rude: say *όχι, ευχαριστώ* or *μάλλον όχι*.
- **Greeklish in e-mail** looks unprofessional. And Greeklish *8* is θ, not 'eight' as in English *gr8*.
- **καμένος** is ambiguous: *είναι καμένος* can mean he is crazy, he is fried, or literally burnt. Context decides.

blocks.title: «Η κόρη μου μιλάει άλλη γλώσσα»: ένα ποστ σε φόρουμ γονιών
blocks.text:
Πόσταρα χθες ένα ποστ στο φόρουμ των γονιών και το αντιγράφω εδώ, γιατί θέλω να μου πείτε αν είμαι υπερβολική.

Έχω μια κόρη δεκαέξι χρονών, τη Δάφνη. Μέχρι πέρσι μου μιλούσε ελληνικά. Φέτος μου μιλάει κάτι άλλο. Χθες στο τραπέζι μου είπε ότι η καθηγήτρια των μαθηματικών «φλεξάρει» με τα ταξίδια της και ότι αυτό είναι «τρελό κριντζ». Τη ρώτησα τι εννοεί και μου απάντησε «τσίλαρε, μαμά, απλά λέω». Μετά μου εξήγησε ότι η κολλητή της είναι «ντελούλου», γιατί πιστεύει ότι ένα αγόρι από το άλλο τμήμα τη γουστάρει, ενώ εκείνος «της έκανε γκόστινγκ» και την άφησε στο σιν τρεις μέρες. Εγώ στην ηλικία της θα έλεγα απλά ότι η φίλη μου είχε κάψα και ότι ο τύπος ήταν ξενέρωτος.

Στο κινητό είναι ακόμα χειρότερα. Της στέλνω «Πού είσαι; Να έρθω να σε πάρω;» και μου απαντάει «πλατεια, κκ, πρμν». Τρία λεπτά μετά: «ν». Ένα σκέτο ν. Της έγραψα «Τι θα πει ν;» και μου έστειλε ένα φωνητικό που γελούσε και έλεγε «ναι, μαμά, ναι, λολ». Ο άντρας μου λέει να μην αγχώνομαι, ότι κι εμείς γράφαμε σε γκρίκλις και λέγαμε «γαμάτο» και «τα σπάει», και ότι οι γονείς μας έπαθαν το ίδιο σοκ. Έχει δίκιο, μάλλον.

Το χειρότερο όμως ήταν την Κυριακή. Προσπάθησα να μιλήσω στη γλώσσα της. Της είπα «Μπρο, πάμε για φρέντο;». Με κοίταξε σαν να είχα τρελαθεί και είπε «Μαμά, άκυρο. Αυτό ήταν το πιο κριντζ πράγμα που έχω ακούσει στη ζωή μου». Μετά το είπε στις φίλες της και τώρα όλες με λένε «μπρο».

Οπότε, ερώτηση: να το αφήσω να περάσει; Να της ζητήσω να μιλάει «κανονικά»; Ή να μάθω κι εγώ τι σημαίνει βασική και μπιφ για να καταλαβαίνω τι γίνεται στο σπίτι μου; Τέσπα, περιμένω τις απαντήσεις σας. Και σας παρακαλώ, όχι σε γκρίκλις.

ΑΠΑΝΤΗΣΗ (Κατερίνα_74): Χαχαχα, πέθανα! Το ίδιο κι εδώ. Ο γιος μου λέει ότι «σαπίζει» όταν κάθεται στον καναπέ. Άσ' τη να μιλάει όπως θέλει, σε δύο χρόνια θα λένε άλλες λέξεις. Απλώς μην ξαναπείς «μπρο». Ποτέ. Τέπο, όπως λένε κι αυτοί.
blocks.en:
I posted this yesterday on the parents' forum and I'm copying it here, because I want you to tell me whether I'm overreacting.

I have a sixteen-year-old daughter, Dafni. Until last year she spoke Greek to me. This year she speaks something else. Yesterday at the table she told me that her maths teacher 'flexes' with her travels and that this is 'crazy cringe'. I asked her what she meant and she answered 'chill, Mum, I'm just saying'. Then she explained that her best friend is 'delulu', because she believes a boy from the other class fancies her, while he 'ghosted' her and left her on seen for three days. At her age I would simply have said that my friend had a crush and that the guy was a bore.

On the phone it's even worse. I text her 'Where are you? Shall I come and pick you up?' and she answers 'square, ok, wait'. Three minutes later: 'y'. A bare 'y'. I wrote 'What does y mean?' and she sent me a voice message laughing and saying 'yes, Mum, yes, lol'. My husband tells me not to stress, that we too typed in Greeklish and said 'γαμάτο' and 'τα σπάει', and that our parents got the same shock. He's probably right.

The worst, though, was on Sunday. I tried to speak her language. I said to her 'Bro, shall we go for a freddo?'. She looked at me as if I had lost my mind and said 'Mum, no way. That was the most cringe thing I've ever heard in my life'. Then she told her friends and now they all call me 'bro'.

So, question: should I let it go? Should I ask her to speak 'normally'? Or should I learn too what 'basic' and 'beef' mean so that I understand what's going on in my own house? Anyway, I'm waiting for your answers. And please, not in Greeklish.

REPLY (Katerina_74): Hahaha, I'm dead! Same here. My son says he's 'rotting' when he sits on the sofa. Let her talk however she likes; in two years they'll be saying other words. Just never say 'bro' again. Ever. Τέπο, as they say.
